common_name: Olé Bicolor Red Oleander (Pink-and-White Ruffled Evergreen Oleander)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring once nights stay reliably above freezing, choosing a baking-hot spot such as a parking strip or south wall where little else thrives.

directions: Olé Bicolor Red layers irregular white streaking over deep pink petals on each ruffled bloom cluster, a two-tone break from the solid-color oleanders that dominate older plantings. Flowering recurs on new growth through the warm months, so an established plant keeps producing fresh clusters rather than finishing in a single flush. It shrugs off poor, sandy, or compacted soil and extended dry spells once rooted in, making it a practical choice for roadside strips, mass plantings, or informal hedges in hot climates. All plant parts are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where children or grazing animals have easy access, and wear gloves when pruning since the sap can irritate skin.

common_name: El Niño Desert Orchid Chitalpa (Fragrant Purple-Flowered Catalpa-Desert Willow Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant in spring in a sunny, well-drained spot with room to grow into a small multi-stem tree; avoid rich, heavily irrigated beds where this hybrid tends to grow soft and lanky.

directions: El Niño is an intergeneric cross between desert willow and catalpa, producing clusters of fragrant, orchid-like, dark purple flowers from late spring through summer on a fast-growing, deciduous, multi-stem shrub that can be trained into a small flowering tree. Its narrow, willow-like leaves give it a lighter, airier look than a typical catalpa, and the plant copes well with reflected heat from pavement and poor, rocky soil that would stress most ornamentals. Established plants need only occasional supplemental water, and overly fertile or constantly damp soil encourages weak, floppy growth rather than vigorous flowering. Deer largely leave it alone, and it draws bees readily when in bloom.

common_name: Pinball Blizzard Mexican Orange (Compact Fragrant White-Flowered Evergreen Choisya)

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants roughly their mature width apart so the rounded habit can fill in without crowding.

directions: Pinball Blizzard covers its dense, rounded form in clusters of small white flowers each spring, their sweet orange-blossom scent carrying well through the garden. The finely divided, dark green foliage releases a lemony, slightly spicy fragrance when brushed or crushed, adding a second sensory layer beyond the bloom. It holds a tidy shape with little pruning and takes well to light shearing if a crisper outline is wanted near a patio or entry planting. Once established it tolerates short dry spells and resists both rabbit browsing and the disease problems that trouble some broadleaf evergreens.

common_name: Proud Berry Pearl Common Snowberry (Compact White-Berried Native Snowberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average to lean soil; this compact native snowberry needs no special amendment and fits foundation beds or mixed borders.

directions: Proud Berry Pearl is a compact selection of the North American native common snowberry, grown mainly for the heavy clusters of large, pure white berries that weigh down its arching stems from fall into winter, long after the small summer flowers fade. Blue-green foliage provides a cool backdrop through the growing season before the berry display takes over as the main attraction. It adapts to a wide range of soils, including the clay and poor fill common around new construction, and its native origin means local pollinators visit the summer flowers readily. Deer generally avoid it, and the compact, two-foot habit makes it easier to place in smaller gardens than older snowberry cultivars.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in humus-rich, acidic, consistently moist soil beneath high shade from trees, where the zigzagging stems can arch and cascade.

directions: Paisley Pup brings variegated new growth in shifting shades of pink, cream, white, and yellow to a plant normally grown for plain evergreen foliage, with the colors settling toward green and burgundy as leaves mature through the season. Chains of small, fragrant, bell-shaped white flowers hang along the arching, zigzag stems in late spring, echoing the blooms of its heath-family relatives like pieris. It spreads slowly into a mounded, cascading groundcover well suited to woodland edges and shaded slopes, where its compact size fits better than older, taller leucothoe selections. Keep roots cool and evenly moist with an organic mulch, since this species struggles in dry or compacted shade.

planting.note: Set out after the last frost once soil has warmed, in full sun with sharp drainage; in marginal zones grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter.

directions: Chicklet Red is a compact member of the Chicklet tecoma series, producing big, trumpet-shaped red flowers from summer through the first frost on a plant small enough for patios and mixed borders rather than the sprawling size of older esperanza selections. Flowers form on new growth, so plants can be cut back hard in early spring to refresh their shape without sacrificing the coming season's bloom. It shrugs off heat, humidity, and short dry spells once established, and hummingbirds and other pollinators visit the flowers readily. Where winters drop much below freezing, grow it as a container specimen or treat it as an annual, since it holds only light, brief frost.

planting.note: Plant in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the upright stems make good cut material, so give it room away from path edges to arch without interference.

directions: Bubble Up lines its upright stems with dense, spherical clusters of pale pink summer flowers that ripen into glossy purple berries noticeably earlier in the fall than older beautyberry cultivars, extending the berry display before frost cuts the season short. It sets fruit without a second plant for cross-pollination, so a single specimen still produces a full show of berries. The berry-studded stems cut well for fall arrangements, and the shrub's upright, fountain-like habit fits borders and mixed shrub plantings better than wide-spreading beautyberry types. Deer tend to pass it over, and it needs only a late-winter thinning cut since it flowers and fruits on the current season's growth.
